summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide through the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), a law that reaches far beyond marriage. A Human Rights Watch report of October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', records that the SSMPA bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and documents police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it. The statute reinforced criminalisation inherited from the colonial era and no federal law provides protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Penalties escalate sharply in the north. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) states that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Entry into Nigeria therefore carries documented criminal exposure at the point of arrival. In August 2026 the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria warned LGBT+ travellers specifically of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Trans people face lethal violence with official indifference to their identity. In August 2024 the beaten body of 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman and TikToker aged 33, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. Six months later, according to The Dial of February 2025, no suspects had been charged despite that announcement. The case stands as a documented trans-specific killing in which the authorities publicly misgendered the victim and produced no arrest.

Policing operates as extortion against people perceived to be gay. TimesLIVE reported in March 2025 that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt, and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, the stated reason being that he was 'looking gay'. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility well beyond its formal scope.

A decade after the SSMPA came into force, the Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in August 2024 that the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its terms, effectively sanctioning abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and a rise in attacks since its passage.

Dating applications are used as a deliberate trap. The same foundation reported in April 2024 that 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other applications: victims are lured to meetings, then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. This is a documented, targeted crime against queer people, and it bears directly on a visitor who uses dating apps while in Nigeria.

Reports of moves to outlaw gender expression are on the record. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians described fear of legislative proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024 to four counts of Naira abuse and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine. She served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at the time of sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting the discretionary nature of placement; the available record does not state whether she was held in a male or female section. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Enforcement has historically taken the form of mass arrest. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011; mass arrests at social venues include more than 100 party-goers at Asaba in Delta State in June 2018, 57 young men at Egbeda in Lagos in August 2018, the 'Warri 67' at Warri in Delta State in August 2023, and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure, and the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008, after which some were threatened, beaten and stoned.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between formal guarantee and enforcement is wide. Section 17(3)(d) of the Nigerian Constitution nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens, and the Federal Ministry of Education maintains a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on the basis of sexual orientation. No enacted legislation gives either provision general effect, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights.

Social attitudes limit what the law alone would predict. A 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found that only 30% of Nigerians agree that LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing. Mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity, and the central role religious institutions play in education, drive stigmatisation of LGBTQ students.

Official language around trans victims has proved as significant as official action. In the Abuja Area Mama case the police characterisation of the victim as 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' preceded an investigation that produced no charges within six months, which suggests that a reported inquiry should not be read as a protection mechanism.

Nigeria's position is consistent with the wider regional pattern of using colonial-era statutes as the basis for contemporary enforcement, but the addition of Sharia penalties in twelve northern states and the specific warning issued to LGBT+ travellers by the UK foreign office in 2026 place Nigeria among the jurisdictions where a foreign government advises its own citizens of imprisonment and death-penalty risk on grounds of sexual orientation.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ Nigerians face documented barriers to medical care. Many fear seeking treatment or reporting crimes because of the risk of arrest and 'kito' extortion, and activists state that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and their allies to abandon community health and education work. International organisations including Global Rights and The Independent Project have provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training, recorded in the US State Department's 2011 report.

Community self-protection has developed in response to app-based entrapment: counter-measures include exposure forums and sting operations, with one administrator's alert page drawing 43,000 followers.

Employment is a recognised site of harm. LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects, and attacks increased over the decade following the 2014 law.

Young people are heavily targeted by enforcement, as the October 2023 arrest of 76 people at a party in Gombe state indicates, and social gatherings at hotels and private venues have repeatedly produced mass arrests since at least 2007.

Transgender Nigerians report fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing, a measure that would directly affect everyday gender expression in public space.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the available record does not state whether Bobrisky was held in a male or female section at Kirikiri, so prison placement for trans women in Nigeria cannot be described from this inventory beyond the finding that placement is discretionary and that maximum-security placement of a first-time offender was found unlawful under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

Unresolved: whether the legislative proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported in September 2022 were introduced or enacted is not sourced here; only the reported fear among transgender Nigerians is documented.

Unresolved: this inventory does not address gender-marker or document rules, passport or visa screening of transgender travellers, airport or border checks that could disclose gender history, or consular protection arrangements. Nothing in the sources allows a finding either way on those entry-screening questions.

Unresolved: outcomes of the mass arrests listed are not fully sourced. Only the Bauchi 2007 group is recorded as having spent years in pre-trial detention before a trial that dissolved by end-2011; conviction, release or acquittal in the Asaba, Egbeda, Warri and Gombe cases is not stated.

Unresolved: enforcement intensity in the twelve northern states under Sharia provisions versus the southern states under the SSMPA is described in the sources at the level of law rather than comparative arrest statistics. Several of the claims above rest on Wikipedia country and biography coverage, which is secondary and unattributed in places, and should be treated as lower-confidence than the Human Rights Watch, UK Home Office and news-agency material.
